case_name: Harminder Kaur and Others v Union Of India & Ors.
facts: The appellants are school teachers who were appointed by the Education Department of Chandigarh Administration on a contract basis.
They had been continuing in their posts for a long time and had fulfilled the requisite educational qualification.
Their services are governed by Chandigarh Education Service (School Cadre) (Group 'C') Recruitment Rules, 1991.

Appellants filed applications for regularization before the Central Administrative Tribunal (Tribunal) on the premise that the respondent - Administration could not have issued fresh advertisement for appointment of teachers.
The said applications were allowed only to the extent that they may not be replaced or substituted by another set of teachers appointed on contract basis.

By order dated 27.8.2003, the Tribunal dismissed the original application opining that they had no right to be regularized in service and their appointment has to come to an end on their replacement by regularly selected teachers.
The respondent - Administration directed appointment of teachers on deputation basis from the States of Punjab and Haryana by an order dated 15.9.2003.
Appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the judgment and order dated 27.8.2003 passed by the Tribunal.
issues: What is the scope of relaxation under Rule 6 of the Rules?
Can the appointments be regularized despite being made on a contract basis?
Is long service a ground for directing regularization?
petitioner_arguments: The appellants were entitled to be absorbed in the services of the Education Department.
Their appointment should have been or could be directed to be regularized.
The principles stated at Paragraph 62 of the decision of the Constitution Bench in Secretary, State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006) 4 SCC 1. should be applied.
respondent_arguments: The appointments were made strictly in terms of contract by contract.
No doubt, for the said purpose an office order had been issued.
It is, however, beyond any doubt or dispute that they had been appointed only for a specified period.

The power conferred on the Heads of the School to engage Lecturers, Masters/Mistresses was for a limited purpose, namely, when the incumbent has proceeded on leave or is not available for teaching beyond 45 days and when no substitute could be provided for in terms of the Rules.
court_reasoning: The court held that long service by itself may not be a ground for directing regularization.
Regularization as is well known is not a mode of appointment.
When appointments in public office are required to be made, the provisions of Arts. 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India are required to be scrupulously followed.
The court referred to a few decisions of this Court and noted that the matter has since been considered by a Constitution Bench of this Court in Uma Devi (2006) 4 SCC 1.

It was held that adherence to the rule of equality in public employment is a basic feature of our Constitution and since the rule of law is the core of our Constitution, a court would certainly be disabled from passing an order upholding a violation of Art. 14 or in ordering the overlooking of the need to comply with the requirements of Art. 14 read with Art. 16 of the Constitution.
holding: The appointments were made strictly in terms of contract by contract.
No doubt, for the said purpose an office order had been issued.
It is, however, beyond any doubt or dispute that they had been appointed only for a specified period.
The court held that long service by itself may not be a ground for directing regularization.
Regularization as is well known is not a mode of appointment.
When appointments in public office are required to be made, the provisions of Arts. 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India are required to be scrupulously followed.
